subject: ELA
title: English Language Arts 6
description: Grade 6 ELA builds close reading of literature and nonfiction, evidence-based writing in all three types (narrative, explanatory, argument), and middle-school grammar and vocabulary. Students read classic short stories, the survival novel Hatchet, Greek myths and the Odyssey, poetry, Helen Keller's autobiography, a Shakespeare comedy and The Secret Garden, then finish with a research project. Grammar (pronouns, punctuation of nonrestrictive elements, sentence variety), Greek and Latin roots, and speaking and listening are woven into every week.
framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts/Literacy; 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.6.1: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.6.2: Determine a theme or central idea and how it is conveyed through details; summarize without personal opinions.
standards.RL.6.3: Describe how a plot unfolds in episodes and how characters respond or change as the plot moves toward resolution.
standards.RL.6.4: Determine meanings of words and phrases, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
standards.RL.6.5: Analyze how a sentence, chapter, scene or stanza fits into the overall structure and contributes to theme, setting or plot.
standards.RL.6.6: Explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker.
standards.RL.6.7: Compare and contrast reading a story, drama or poem with listening to or viewing an audio, video or live version.
standards.RL.6.9: Compare and contrast texts in different forms or genres in terms of their approaches to similar themes and topics.
standards.RL.6.10: Read and comprehend grade 6-8 literature, including stories, dramas and poems, proficiently.
standards.RI.6.1: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.6.2: Determine a central idea and how it is conveyed through details; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.6.3: Analyze how a key individual, event or idea is introduced, illustrated and elaborated in a text.
standards.RI.6.4: Determine meanings of words and phrases in informational text, including figurative, connotative and technical meanings.
standards.RI.6.5: Analyze how a sentence, paragraph, chapter or section fits into the overall structure of a text.
standards.RI.6.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and explain how it is conveyed.
standards.RI.6.7: Integrate information presented in different media or formats as well as in words.
standards.RI.6.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing supported from unsupported claims.
standards.RI.6.9: Compare and contrast one author's presentation of events with that of another (e.g., memoir vs. biography).
standards.RI.6.10: Read and comprehend grade 6-8 literary nonfiction proficiently.
standards.W.6.1: Write arguments supporting claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
standards.W.6.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas through relevant content.
standards.W.6.3: Write narratives developing real or imagined experiences using effective technique, descriptive details and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.6.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose and audience.
standards.W.6.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach.
standards.W.6.6: Use technology to produce and publish writing and to interact with others; type a minimum of three pages in one sitting.
standards.W.6.7: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing as appropriate.
standards.W.6.8: Gather relevant information from print and digital sources, assess credibility, quote or paraphrase, and provide bibliographic information.
standards.W.6.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
standards.W.6.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks and purposes.
standards.SL.6.1: Engage effectively in collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing one's own clearly.
standards.SL.6.2: Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats and explain how it contributes to a topic.
standards.SL.6.3: Delineate a speaker's argument and claims, distinguishing supported from unsupported claims.
standards.SL.6.4: Present claims and findings, sequencing ideas logically with pertinent details; use appropriate eye contact, volume and pronunciation.
standards.SL.6.5: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations to clarify information.
standards.SL.6.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.6.1: Demonstrate command of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
standards.L.6.1a: Ensure that pronouns are in the proper case (subjective, objective, possessive).
standards.L.6.1c: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person.
standards.L.6.1d: Recognize and correct vague pronouns (unclear or ambiguous antecedents).
standards.L.6.1e: Recognize variations from standard English in writing and speaking and use strategies to improve expression.
standards.L.6.2: Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation and spelling when writing.
standards.L.6.2a: Use commas, parentheses or dashes to set off nonrestrictive or parenthetical elements.
standards.L.6.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions; vary sentence patterns for meaning, interest and style; maintain consistency in style and tone.
standards.L.6.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown words using context, affixes and roots, and reference materials.
standards.L.6.4b: Use common grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to meaning (e.g., audience, auditory, audible).
standards.L.6.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships and nuances in word meanings (personification, connotation).
standards.L.6.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: Short Stories and Personal Narrative
units.big_idea: Authors build plot, character and suspense through deliberate choices we can imitate in our own narratives.

units.title: Survival: Hatchet Novel Study
units.big_idea: Facing adversity changes people; fiction and nonfiction together show how humans survive.

units.title: Myths, Heroes and the Odyssey
units.big_idea: Ancient myths and epics carry themes about courage, pride and home that still shape our language and stories.

units.title: Argument: Claims and Evidence
units.big_idea: Strong arguments make clear claims supported by relevant, credible evidence and fair reasoning.

units.title: Poetry: Sound, Image and Meaning
units.big_idea: Poets compress meaning into images, sounds and structure; figurative language shapes tone.

units.title: Memoir and Biography: Helen Keller
units.big_idea: Writers of memoir shape their own story; comparing memoir and biography reveals point of view.

units.title: Drama: A Midsummer Night's Dream
units.big_idea: Plays are written to be performed; staging, voice and movement bring the text's comedy and conflict to life.

units.title: Novel Study: The Secret Garden
units.big_idea: Characters and settings can transform together; a theme emerges from how characters change.

units.title: Research and Presentation
units.big_idea: Researchers ask focused questions, evaluate sources, synthesize information and share it clearly.

objectives: Map the plot structure of a short story
materials: 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' by Rudyard Kipling (from The Jungle Book)

days.title: Reader's notebook launch
days.work: Set up a reader's notebook, write a reading-history page, and read the first third of 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi', jotting predictions about the cobras.

days.title: Character and evidence
days.work: Finish the story; list three traits of Rikki with a quoted line of evidence for each, and practice the 'claim + quote + explain' paragraph frame.

days.title: Plot mountain
days.work: Draw a plot diagram of the story and mark where Kipling builds suspense; discuss with a parent which moment is the climax and why.

days.title: Pronoun case
days.work: Lesson on subjective, objective and possessive pronouns; correct 15 sentences (e.g., 'Him and me went') and find 5 pronouns in the story.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a one-paragraph response explaining how Rikki changes from beginning to end, citing two quotations; take a 10-item pronoun-case quiz.

weeks.assessment: Evidence paragraph on character plus pronoun-case quiz.

weeks.topic: Irony and point of view: O. Henry and Saki
objectives: Explain how narration affects what readers know
materials: 'The Ransom of Red Chief' and 'After Twenty Years' by O. Henry

days.title: Situational irony
days.work: Read 'The Ransom of Red Chief' and chart what the kidnappers expect vs. what happens; write two sentences explaining the irony.

days.title: Narrator's voice
days.work: Analyze how Sam's first-person narration and fancy vocabulary create humor; rewrite one paragraph in plain third person and compare the effect.

days.title: Twist endings
days.work: Read 'After Twenty Years' and 'The Open Window'; mark foreshadowing clues on a second read and discuss which twist was fairer to the reader.

days.title: Context clues
days.work: Use context clues to define 10 challenging words from the O. Henry stories, then verify with a dictionary.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a short comparison of how two of the three stories use point of view to surprise readers; quiz on irony and pronoun case.

objectives: Plan a personal narrative around a meaningful moment
Use dialogue, pacing and sensory detail

days.title: Finding a story
days.work: Brainstorm a heart map of memorable moments, choose one small moment, and tell it aloud to a listener in two minutes.

days.title: Strong leads
days.work: Study leads from the unit's stories and write three possible openings for your narrative (action, dialogue, setting).

days.title: Drafting with dialogue
days.work: Draft the middle of your narrative, including at least four lines of correctly punctuated dialogue.

days.title: Slow-motion moment
days.work: Expand the most important moment with sensory detail and inner thoughts so it takes up at least a full paragraph.

days.title: Ending and reflection
days.work: Draft an ending that reflects on why the moment mattered and read the full draft aloud for a family member's feedback.

weeks.assessment: Complete draft checked against a narrative checklist.

objectives: Revise for sentence variety and word choice
Edit for pronoun use and punctuation

days.title: Sentence variety
days.work: Lesson on varying sentence beginnings and lengths; revise ten sentences in your draft so no two consecutive sentences start the same way.

days.title: Word choice
days.work: Replace weak verbs and vague nouns with precise ones; highlight five improvements in a different color.

days.title: Editing conference
days.work: Edit with a checklist for pronoun case, dialogue punctuation, capitalization and spelling, then conference with a parent.

days.title: Publish
days.work: Type the final narrative (at least 2 pages) and add a title.

days.title: Author's chair and check
days.work: Read your narrative aloud with expression to an audience and score it with the narrative rubric; take a unit vocabulary quiz.

weeks.assessment: Published personal narrative scored on a 4-point rubric.

days.title: Before the crash
days.work: Read chapter 1, locate the flight route on a map of Canada, and note what we learn about Brian and the Secret.

days.title: Crash landing
days.work: Read chapters 2-3; list sensory words Paulsen uses during the crash and explain how short sentences build tension.

days.title: First night
days.work: Read chapter 4; make a T-chart of Brian's physical and emotional problems and discuss which is worse.

days.title: Intensive pronouns
days.work: Lesson on intensive pronouns (himself, myself); write 8 sentences about Brian using them correctly and fix 6 misuse errors.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading check quiz on chapters 1-4 and a journal entry from Brian's point of view after the first night.

weeks.assessment: Reading quiz and point-of-view journal entry.

objectives: Read informational text on survival priorities
materials: ReadWorks or CommonLit wilderness survival article

days.title: Shelter and food
days.work: Read chapters 5-6 and list Brian's survival decisions with page numbers; rate each decision smart or risky.

days.title: Self-pity
days.work: Read chapters 7-8; write a paragraph explaining Brian's lesson that self-pity 'didn't work', citing two quotes.

days.title: Fire
days.work: Read chapter 9 and annotate how Paulsen describes fire as a 'friend'; identify personification.

days.title: Survival nonfiction
days.work: Read a wilderness-survival article and the Ten Essentials list, then summarize the central idea objectively in 4-5 sentences.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Compare Brian's priorities with the article's advice in a Venn diagram and take a chapters 5-9 reading quiz.

days.title: Foolbirds and fish
days.work: Read chapters 10-11 and record what Brian learns from failure while hunting; connect to the idea of 'tough hope'.

days.title: The plane passes
days.work: Read chapter 12 and write a journal entry analyzing how the missed rescue plane is a turning point.

days.title: New Brian
days.work: Read chapter 13 and complete a 'Brian then vs. now' character-change chart with evidence.

days.title: Pronoun shifts
days.work: Lesson on shifts in pronoun number and person; correct 12 sentences such as 'If a person gets lost, you should stay calm'.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Draft a theme statement for Hatchet (not just a topic word) and support it with three details; quiz on chapters 10-13.

days.title: The moose and the tornado
days.work: Read chapters 14-15 and explain how these setbacks test the 'new Brian'.

days.title: Back to the plane
days.work: Read chapters 16-17; list the items in the survival pack and predict how they will change his life.

days.title: Rescue
days.work: Read chapters 18-19 and the epilogue; discuss how the epilogue changes our understanding of the story's ending.

days.title: Listen and compare
days.work: Listen to a chapter of the audiobook while following along and note what the narrator's voice adds or changes.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take the final Hatchet comprehension test with short constructed responses.

objectives: Write an explanatory essay with evidence from fiction and nonfiction

days.title: Thesis and plan
days.work: Write a thesis explaining three ways Brian survives (mental and physical) and fill an essay organizer with evidence.

days.title: Body paragraphs
days.work: Draft three body paragraphs, each with a quote from Hatchet and one fact from the survival article.

days.title: Intro and conclusion
days.work: Draft an introduction with a hook and a conclusion that explains what Brian's survival teaches readers.

days.title: Revise and edit
days.work: Revise for transitions and precise words; edit for pronoun shifts and intensive pronouns, then type the final essay.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Submit the essay, self-score with the explanatory rubric, and take the unit vocabulary test.

weeks.assessment: Explanatory essay scored on rubric; vocabulary test.

objectives: Use Greek and Latin roots to determine meaning
materials: 'A Wonder-Book' and 'Tanglewood Tales' by Nathaniel Hawthorne (Project Gutenberg)
D'Aulaires' Book of Greek Myths (library, optional)

days.title: Why myths?
days.work: Read the myth of Prometheus and list what it explains (fire, human suffering); discuss why cultures created myths.

days.title: Pandora's box
days.work: Read Hawthorne's 'The Paradise of Children' (Pandora) and write the theme in one sentence with supporting evidence.

days.title: Midas and hubris
days.work: Read 'The Golden Touch' (King Midas) and analyze how Midas's choices drive the plot to its resolution.

days.title: Words from myths
days.work: Study roots and words from myths (narcissist, echo, panic, tantalize, chronology, psyche) and build a 20-word root map.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on myth themes and roots; retell a myth orally to a family member in two minutes.

materials: 'The Children's Homer' by Padraic Colum (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Meet Odysseus
days.work: Read the opening of the Odysseus section of The Children's Homer, map the start of his journey, and list epic hero traits.

days.title: The Cyclops
days.work: Read the Polyphemus episode and cite evidence that Odysseus is both clever and proud.

days.title: Aeolus and Circe
days.work: Read the bag of winds and Circe episodes and explain how the crew's choices cause new problems.

days.title: Root review
days.work: Find 10 words in the reading with Greek or Latin parts (e.g., 'journey', 'monstrous') and analyze them.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph analyzing which episode best shows Odysseus's greatest flaw; reading quiz.

objectives: Compare text with a film or audio version
materials: audio or animated clip of the Sirens episode

days.title: Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis
days.work: Read the Sirens and Scylla episodes and discuss what they suggest about temptation and leadership.

days.title: Return to Ithaca
days.work: Read Odysseus's return in disguise and trace how Penelope tests him.

days.title: Themes across the epic
days.work: Write two theme statements for the Odyssey (e.g., about loyalty or pride) with evidence.

days.title: Text vs. media
days.work: Watch or listen to a retelling of the Sirens episode and compare it with the text in a chart of what was added, cut or changed.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a comparison of how a Greek myth and the Odyssey both treat pride (RL.6.9) and take the Odyssey quiz.

weeks.topic: Writing: modern myth or hero's journey story
objectives: Write a narrative using hero's-journey structure
Use precise language and transitions to show time shifts

days.title: Hero's journey
days.work: Map Odysseus's and Brian's stories onto the hero's journey and plan your own hero's journey story or modern myth.

days.title: Draft beginning
days.work: Draft your story's opening and call to adventure using vivid setting details.

days.title: Draft trials
days.work: Draft two trials your hero faces, using dialogue and transitions that show time shifts.

days.title: Revise and edit
days.work: Revise the climax and return; edit for pronoun case and consistent verb tense, then type the final draft.

days.title: Share and check
days.work: Read your story aloud and score it with the narrative rubric; take the unit test on myths and the Odyssey.

weeks.assessment: Narrative scored on rubric; unit test.

materials: CommonLit argument articles (e.g., on school start times, homework, screen time)

days.title: What is an argument?
days.work: Compare a fact, an opinion and an argument; identify the claim in 6 short advertisements and op-ed excerpts.

days.title: Claim, reasons, evidence
days.work: Read an article on whether middle schools should start later and annotate the claim, reasons and evidence in three colors.

days.title: Supported or not?
days.work: Evaluate each piece of evidence in a second article as relevant, sufficient or unsupported and explain why.

days.title: Author's purpose and bias
days.work: Determine each author's point of view and identify loaded words that reveal bias.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Read a new short argument and complete an argument-analysis organizer independently as a quiz.

objectives: Write a clear claim and gather evidence
materials: two to three articles on a chosen issue (e.g., Should zoos exist? Should kids have phones?)

days.title: Choose a question
days.work: Choose a debatable question from a list, read two articles on it, and take a position.

days.title: Evidence notes
days.work: Take notes on cards, separating quotations and paraphrases, with source titles.

days.title: Vague pronouns
days.work: Lesson on vague pronouns ('they say', 'this'); fix 12 sentences with unclear antecedents.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Outline an essay with a claim, two or three reasons, evidence for each and a counterclaim with rebuttal.

days.title: Check-in
days.work: Explain your outline orally to a parent in 3 minutes and revise based on their questions; quiz on vague pronouns.

objectives: Draft an argument essay with formal style

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft an introduction with a hook, background and a precise claim.

days.title: Body paragraphs
days.work: Draft body paragraphs that explain how each piece of evidence supports your reason.

days.title: Counterclaim
days.work: Draft a counterclaim-and-rebuttal paragraph and a conclusion that follows from the argument.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise for formal style (no slang, no 'I think') and add transitions like 'furthermore' and 'however'.

days.title: Edit and publish
days.work: Edit for pronoun use, commas and spelling and type the final essay; self-score with the argument rubric.

materials: a recorded student speech or TED-Ed talk

days.title: Evaluate a speech
days.work: Watch a short persuasive speech and note the speaker's claims and whether each is supported.

days.title: Prepare a speech
days.work: Turn your essay into a 2-minute opening statement with note cards.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Practice delivery (eye contact, volume, pace) while recording yourself and critique the video.

days.title: Debate
days.work: Hold a structured debate with a family member or co-op partner: opening statements, rebuttals and closings.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a reflection on the debate and take the unit test on argument terms and analysis.

weeks.assessment: Debate performance rubric and unit test.

objectives: Identify simile, metaphor, personification and hyperbole
Explain how figurative language affects meaning
materials: 'Hope is the thing with feathers' by Emily Dickinson

days.title: Images
days.work: Read 'Fog' and sketch the image it creates; identify the metaphor and explain what it suggests about fog.

days.title: Extended metaphor
days.work: Read Dickinson's 'Hope is the thing with feathers' and annotate each stanza's development of the bird metaphor.

days.title: Hughes's dreams
days.work: Read Hughes's 'Dreams' and 'Mother to Son'; compare their metaphors and tones.

days.title: Connotation
days.work: Sort word pairs by connotation (thrifty/stingy, slender/skinny) and rewrite a stanza changing connotations to alter tone.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write your own poem using an extended metaphor; quiz on figurative language identification.

weeks.assessment: Figurative language quiz and original poem.

objectives: Explain how stanza structure contributes to meaning
materials: 'Paul Revere's Ride' by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

days.title: Rhythm
days.work: Read 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud and tap the galloping meter; explain how rhythm matches content.

days.title: Rhyme scheme
days.work: Label rhyme schemes of three poems and identify alliteration and internal rhyme in an excerpt of 'The Raven'.

days.title: Heard vs. read
days.work: Listen to a professional recording of 'The Raven' excerpt and compare it with your silent reading.

days.title: Structure
days.work: Analyze how one stanza of 'Paul Revere's Ride' builds suspense within the whole poem.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Memorize and recite 12+ lines of a chosen poem with expression; quiz on sound devices.

materials: 'The Road Not Taken' by Robert Frost
'Who Has Seen the Wind?' by Christina Rossetti
'The Land of Counterpane' by Robert Louis Stevenson

days.title: The speaker
days.work: Read 'The Road Not Taken' and describe the speaker's situation and attitude with evidence.

days.title: Theme in Frost
days.work: Debate the poem's theme (is it really about choosing the 'less traveled' road?) and write a theme paragraph.

days.title: Tone words
days.work: Read Rossetti and Stevenson poems, choose precise tone words for each, and cite the lines that create that tone.

days.title: Free verse
days.work: Read a free-verse poem from CommonLit and compare its structure with Frost's rhymed stanzas.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Analyze an unseen poem independently for speaker, tone and theme as a quiz.

days.title: Ode
days.work: Write an ode to an ordinary object using at least three types of figurative language.

days.title: Haiku and concrete poems
days.work: Write three haiku about nature observations and one concrete (shape) poem.

days.title: Narrative poem
days.work: Write a short narrative poem with a rhyme scheme, modeled on Longfellow.

days.title: Compile
days.work: Revise and compile 6-8 poems into an illustrated anthology with a table of contents and author's note.

days.title: Poetry cafe
days.work: Host a family poetry reading performing three poems; take the unit test on poetry terms.

weeks.assessment: Anthology rubric, performance and unit test.

weeks.topic: The Story of My Life, chapters 1-4
objectives: Determine how an author introduces key ideas and events
Analyze point of view in autobiography
materials: 'The Story of My Life' by Helen Keller (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Early childhood
days.work: Read chapters 1-2 and list how Keller introduces her illness and frustrations; note how the adult Keller looks back on her child self.

days.title: The 'water' moment
days.work: Read chapters 3-4 and analyze the water-pump moment: how does Keller's word choice show it was life-changing?

days.title: Commas, parentheses, dashes
days.work: Lesson on setting off nonrestrictive and parenthetical elements; punctuate 15 sentences about Keller three ways and discuss the effect.

days.title: Point of view
days.work: Write a paragraph on Keller's purpose in writing her autobiography, with two quotations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz on chapters 1-4 and punctuation quiz.

weeks.topic: The Story of My Life, selected chapters 5-23
objectives: Trace the development of a central idea

days.title: Learning language
days.work: Read chapters 5-7 and trace how Anne Sullivan teaches Keller, listing each method.

days.title: Braille and reading
days.work: Read about Keller learning to read and write; use a Braille chart to write your name with glue dots on cardstock.

days.title: Learning to speak
days.work: Read chapter 13 on learning to speak and explain how this section contributes to the central idea.

days.title: Objective summary
days.work: Write a 150-word objective summary of the selections read so far.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on central idea and structure; discuss with a parent what surprised you most.

objectives: Compare how different authors present the same events
Compare text with a filmed or staged version
materials: a children's biography of Helen Keller (library)
film clip of the water-pump scene from 'The Miracle Worker' (1962)

days.title: Biography account
days.work: Read a biography's account of the water-pump scene and annotate differences from Keller's own account.

days.title: Compare authors
days.work: Complete a comparison chart: what each author includes, omits and emphasizes, and why.

days.title: Film scene
days.work: Watch the water-pump scene from 'The Miracle Worker' and note how actors, sound and camera change the experience.

days.title: Primary sources
days.work: Look at Library of Congress photographs and letters related to Helen Keller and explain what they add.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 3-paragraph comparison of memoir vs. biography vs. film versions of the same event.

objectives: Write a memoir chapter about a time you learned something hard

days.title: Plan
days.work: Brainstorm moments when you learned something difficult and plan a memoir chapter with a turning point.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft the chapter, combining narration of events with adult-like reflection, as Keller does.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise for voice and add at least three nonrestrictive elements punctuated with commas, parentheses or dashes.

days.title: Edit and publish
days.work: Edit for conventions and publish the chapter typed.

days.title: Share and check
days.work: Read your chapter aloud and take the unit test on informational reading skills.

weeks.assessment: Memoir chapter rubric and unit test.

weeks.topic: Shakespeare's world and A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 1-2
materials: 'Tales from Shakespeare' by Charles and Mary Lamb (Project Gutenberg)
Folger Shakespeare text of A Midsummer Night's Dream (free online)

days.title: Shakespeare's theater
days.work: Learn about the Globe Theatre and Elizabethan stage; read the Lambs' prose retelling of the play for an overview.

days.title: The lovers
days.work: Read Act 1 Scene 1 in the original (with glosses); chart the four lovers and their conflicts.

days.title: The mechanicals
days.work: Read Act 1 Scene 2 aloud in parts and identify what makes the actors' rehearsal funny.

days.title: The fairies
days.work: Read key speeches from Act 2 (Puck, Oberon) and paraphrase three passages into modern English.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Complete a plotline web connecting the lovers, fairies and mechanicals; quiz on drama terms.

weeks.assessment: Drama terms quiz and plot web.

objectives: Analyze how scenes build comic conflict

days.title: Love potion chaos
days.work: Read selected scenes from Act 3 and chart who loves whom before and after the potion.

days.title: Bottom's transformation
days.work: Read the Bottom and Titania scene aloud and identify puns and wordplay.

days.title: Resolution
days.work: Read Act 4 and the Pyramus and Thisbe performance in Act 5; explain how each plotline resolves.

days.title: Play vs. retelling
days.work: Compare the Lambs' prose version with Shakespeare's play: what is lost and gained? Write two paragraphs.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a comprehension quiz and write a short analysis of how one scene contributes to the play's comedy.

objectives: Perform a scene with appropriate voice and movement
Compare live or filmed performance to the text

days.title: View a performance
days.work: Watch a filmed scene of the play and compare the director's choices with your mental picture from reading.

days.title: Cut and cast
days.work: Choose and cut a 2-3 minute scene (e.g., the mechanicals' rehearsal), assign roles with family members, and mark blocking.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Rehearse lines with attention to iambic rhythm, projection and gestures.

days.title: Perform
days.work: Perform and record the scene for an audience.

days.title: Reflect and check
days.work: Write a reflection explaining your interpretive choices with textual evidence; take the unit test.

weeks.assessment: Performance rubric, reflection and unit test.

objectives: Describe Mary's character at the start
materials: 'The Secret Garden' by Frances Hodgson Burnett (Project Gutenberg or library)

days.title: Mistress Mary
days.work: Read chapters 1-2 and list Mary's traits and their causes with evidence.

days.title: Across the moor
days.work: Read chapters 3-4 and describe Misselthwaite Manor and the moor; explain how the setting reflects Mary's mood.

days.title: Yorkshire dialect
days.work: Read chapter 5; translate five lines of Martha's dialect and discuss why Burnett uses dialect.

days.title: The key
days.work: Read chapters 6-7 and predict how finding the garden will change Mary.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a character sketch of Mary with three quotations; reading quiz on chapters 1-7.

objectives: Explain how the narrator develops point of view

days.title: Inside the garden
days.work: Read chapters 8-10 and note sensory images of the garden coming alive; compare to Mary's changes.

days.title: Dickon
days.work: Read chapters 11-12 and analyze Dickon's role and how others respond to him.

days.title: Colin
days.work: Read chapters 13-14 and compare Colin with Mary at the beginning of the book.

days.title: Narrator
days.work: Read chapter 15; find places where the omniscient narrator comments directly, and discuss how that shapes our view.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Book-club style discussion of three questions you prepared; quiz on chapters 8-15.

days.title: Colin's tantrum
days.work: Read chapters 16-19 and explain how Mary's response to Colin shows her growth.

days.title: Into the garden
days.work: Read chapters 20-22 and identify the garden as a symbol of healing.

days.title: Magic
days.work: Read chapters 23-25 and discuss what the children mean by 'Magic'.

days.title: Homecoming
days.work: Read chapters 26-27 and compare the ending with the opening chapters.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write two theme statements for the novel and take the final novel test.

objectives: Write an argument about a literary text

days.title: Claim
days.work: Write a claim answering: Who changes more, Mary or Colin, and what causes the change? Gather five pieces of evidence.

days.title: Embedding quotes
days.work: Lesson on embedding quotations smoothly; draft two body paragraphs with embedded quotes and analysis.

days.title: Finish draft
days.work: Draft the introduction, a counterclaim paragraph and conclusion.

days.title: Revise and edit
days.work: Revise for sentence variety and consistent formal tone; edit and type the final essay.

days.title: Unit check
days.work: Submit the essay with a self-assessment and take the unit vocabulary test.

materials: Library of Congress and Smithsonian websites

days.title: Choose a topic
days.work: Choose a topic connected to ancient civilizations or science (e.g., how the pyramids were built) and write a focused research question.

days.title: Evaluate sources
days.work: Evaluate six websites with a credibility checklist (author, date, purpose, evidence) and keep the best three.

days.title: Library visit
days.work: Find at least one print book and one database article at the public library on your topic.

days.title: Note-taking
days.work: Take paraphrased notes on cards, each labeled with its source and subtopic.

days.title: Check-in
days.work: Create an MLA-style works-cited list for your sources and refocus your question if needed.

weeks.assessment: Source evaluation sheets and works-cited list.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Sort note cards into 3-4 subtopics and build an outline with headings.

days.title: Draft sections
days.work: Draft two sections, synthesizing information from at least two sources in each.

days.title: Paraphrase practice
days.work: Practice paraphrasing vs. plagiarism with three passages, then draft the remaining sections with in-text citations.

days.title: Text features
days.work: Add an introduction, conclusion and at least one graphic (map, diagram or timeline) with a caption.

days.title: Check-in
days.work: Type the full draft (at least 3 pages in one sitting) and conference with a parent using the research rubric.

objectives: Revise for clarity and precise vocabulary

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise for precise domain-specific vocabulary and logical order of ideas.

days.title: Edit and publish
days.work: Edit for conventions, check every citation, and publish the final report.

days.title: Build slides
days.work: Create 6-8 slides with images and minimal text that clarify your key findings.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Rehearse a 5-minute presentation focusing on eye contact, volume and clear pronunciation.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present to family or co-op and answer audience questions.

objectives: Demonstrate grade 6 reading and writing skills
Reflect on growth as a reader and writer

days.title: Reading assessment
days.work: Read an unfamiliar story and article and answer evidence-based constructed-response questions.

days.title: On-demand writing
days.work: Write a timed argument or explanatory essay from a prompt with two short sources.

days.title: Grammar and vocabulary
days.work: Take a cumulative test on pronouns, punctuation, roots and figurative language.

days.title: Portfolio
days.work: Choose your best three pieces from the year and write a cover letter explaining your growth.

days.title: Looking ahead
days.work: Create a summer reading list of 6 books and share your favorite read of the year in a book talk.

weeks.assessment: Final reading, writing and language assessments; portfolio letter.
